questions.stem: A nurse fulfills ongoing continuing competency requirements, such as continuing education or periodic skills validation, as part of maintaining licensure. The underlying purpose of these requirements is to:

questions.stem: A client has new left lower-quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and altered bowel habits. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings prove appendicitis because fever and abdominal pain identify appendiceal inflammation regardless of the location or other clinical features.","B":"The findings are a normal bowel variation that needs no evaluation because left lower-quadrant pain is not associated with acute colonic disease.","C":"The findings establish diverticulitis without further assessment, so imaging is never useful when a client has not had a prior imaging-confirmed episode.","D":"Acute diverticulitis is a reasonable concern; clinical assessment is required, and CT can confirm the diagnosis or assess complications when indicated."}}
questions.rationale: Left lower-quadrant pain with fever and bowel symptoms is compatible with acute diverticulitis, but symptoms alone are not perfectly specific. CT is commonly used to confirm the diagnosis when it has not previously been imaging-confirmed or when severity or complications need assessment.

questions.source_detail: AGA Best Practice Advice 1: CT should be considered to confirm diverticulitis without prior imaging-confirmed diagnosis; LLQ pain, fever and bowel changes are common but not specific. questions.stem: A client has right upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy sign. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Treat the presentation as uncomplicated dyspepsia without further evaluation, even though a positive Murphy sign raises concern for gallbladder inflammation.","B":"Diagnose acute cholecystitis from symptoms alone and omit imaging, because laboratory testing and imaging cannot improve diagnostic confidence.","C":"Suspect acute cholecystitis and obtain right-upper-quadrant ultrasound as the usual initial imaging study to evaluate the gallbladder and biliary tract.","D":"Use colonoscopy as the first imaging procedure because right-upper-quadrant pain with a Murphy sign primarily indicates colonic rather than biliary disease."}}
questions.rationale: Right upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy sign are compatible with acute cholecystitis. Ultrasound is generally the initial imaging test used to evaluate suspected acute cholecystitis and gallstones; diagnosis incorporates clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings.
questions.source_name: American College of Surgeons — Acute Cholecystitis Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: WSES 2020 guideline Section 1, Statements 1.1–1.3: do not rely on one feature; use combined history/exam/labs/imaging; RUQ pain, fever and Murphy sign are useful features; ultrasound is preferred initial imaging. World J Emerg Surg 2020;15:61, DOI 10.1186/s13017-020-00336-x; currentness reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client with a known history of peptic ulcer disease suddenly develops severe, sharp abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen. The nurse should suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Uncomplicated dyspepsia, because sudden severe pain and a rigid abdomen are expected findings during a routine peptic-ulcer flare.","B":"Perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis and peritoneal signs, a surgical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and management.","C":"Simple constipation, because a board-like abdomen most often reflects stool retention rather than peritoneal irritation.","D":"Musculoskeletal abdominal-wall pain, because ulcer complications do not typically cause abrupt severe pain or guarding."}}
questions.rationale: Sudden, severe, sharp abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen in a client with known peptic ulcer disease is highly concerning for ulcer perforation, a surgical emergency (leading to peritonitis) requiring immediate provider notification and evaluation, distinct from typical, more gradual ulcer-related discomfort.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Peptic Ulcer Disease Complications
questions.source_detail: WSES PPU guideline, Diagnosis section: perforation usually presents with sudden abdominal pain and localized/generalized peritonitis; CT is recommended for suspected perforated peptic ulcer. World J Emerg Surg 2020;15:3, DOI 10.1186/s13017-019-0283-9; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

questions.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation and known vascular disease develops sudden, severe abdominal pain that is notably out of proportion to the physical exam findings, along with nausea and vomiting. The nurse should suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Acute mesenteric ischemia, especially given atrial fibrillation and severe abdominal pain that is disproportionate to early examination findings.","B":"Uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis, because nausea and vomiting make vascular causes of abdominal pain unlikely in this presentation.","C":"Mechanical low-back strain, because pain from the abdominal wall commonly produces severe symptoms despite minimal examination findings.","D":"Stable chronic peripheral vascular disease, because severe new abdominal pain is expected and does not require urgent vascular evaluation in this client."}}
questions.rationale: Sudden, severe abdominal pain that is notably out of proportion to a relatively benign-appearing physical exam, particularly in a client with risk factors such as atrial fibrillation (embolic source) or vascular disease, is a classic warning sign of acute mesenteric ischemia, a vascular emergency requiring immediate evaluation given the significant risk of bowel necrosis if blood flow is not promptly restored.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Acute Mesenteric Ischemia Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: WSES 2022 AMI guideline Statements 1.1 and 1.5: severe pain out of proportion should be assumed AMI until disproven; CTA should be performed without delay; atrial fibrillation is an embolic risk source. World J Emerg Surg 2022;17:54, DOI 10.1186/s13017-022-00443-x; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
